issues: The summary conflates dates: 'In 2011 the first class action ... was brought, and the court held that streaming services could be covered.' The suit was filed in July 2011, but the district court held that Hulu was a 'video tape service provider' on 10 August 2012. HLR footnote 35 cites In re Hulu Privacy Litig., No. C 11-03764, 2012 WL 3282960 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 10, 2012).

The significance rests on the 1988 per-disclosure consent rule. The same HLR page records that the 2012 amendments 'allowed videotape service providers to obtain continuing rather than case-by-case consent', so the summary should say the rule was later loosened.

fieldFixes.summary: The Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988 (Public Law 100-618), approved on 5 November 1988, amended title 18 'to preserve personal privacy with respect to the rental, purchase, or delivery of video tapes or similar audio visual materials'. A video tape service provider that knowingly discloses information identifying a customer as having requested or obtained specific video materials is liable to that customer, unless an exception applies - one being disclosure with the consumer's informed, written consent given at the time the disclosure is sought. Amendments in 2012 let providers obtain continuing rather than case-by-case consent. The first class action under the act against an online service, In re Hulu Privacy Litigation, was brought in July 2011, and in August 2012 the district court held that online video streaming services were covered.
